patient.chief_complaint: Recurrent episodes of staring and unresponsiveness, with one episode witnessed by husband involving involuntary hand movements
patient.history_present_illness:
Ms. Delgado is a 41-year-old right-handed elementary school teacher who presents to the emergency department after her husband witnessed an episode of unresponsiveness accompanied by repetitive fumbling hand movements during dinner the previous evening. He reports that the patient suddenly stopped speaking mid-sentence, stared blankly ahead, and appeared to be picking at the tablecloth with her left hand while making subtle chewing motions with her mouth. The episode lasted approximately 45 to 60 seconds. When she came to, she appeared confused and asked what had happened. She was oriented again within approximately five minutes but reported feeling fatigued and complained of a mild headache.

Upon further questioning, the patient acknowledges that she has been experiencing intermittent spells over the past eight to ten months that she has difficulty describing. She notes that sometimes she will suddenly feel disconnected from her surroundings, as if she is observing herself from the outside, along with a vague uncomfortable sensation in her abdomen that she cannot further characterize. These episodes are brief, typically lasting 20 to 40 seconds, and she is generally able to continue with what she is doing afterward, though she sometimes feels momentarily foggy. She estimates these have occurred approximately once or twice per month. She initially attributed them to her anxiety disorder and discussed them with her primary care physician, who increased her sertraline dose from 25 mg to 50 mg about four months ago without clear improvement in the episodes. She denies any convulsive activity, urinary incontinence, or tongue biting during these events, though she does mention the occasional cheek biting noted on waking. She has not experienced any clear preceding headache, visual changes, or focal weakness. There is no history of head trauma, CNS infection, or prior neuroimaging. She notes that her sleep has been somewhat disrupted due to work-related stress but denies significant sleep deprivation. There was no recent illness or medication changes other than the sertraline adjustment.

output.query: temporal lobe epilepsy misdiagnosed as anxiety disorder panic attacks

results.title: Differential diagnosis of paroxysmal episodes in adults: focal seizures versus panic disorder
results.source: Vazquez B, Devinsky O. Epilepsy & Behavior 2003;4(6):715-719
results.summary: Temporal lobe seizures with prominent autonomic and emotional features (fear, epigastric sensation, depersonalization) are frequently misdiagnosed as panic attacks. Average delay to correct diagnosis ranges from 1 to 7 years.

results.title: The role of prolonged video-EEG monitoring in diagnosis of paroxysmal events
results.summary: Approximately 20-30% of patients referred to epilepsy monitoring units for refractory seizures are found to have non-epileptic events. Conversely, some patients with anxiety or panic disorder diagnoses are found to have temporal lobe epilepsy on prolonged monitoring.

results.title: Subtle MRI-negative temporal lobe epilepsy: importance of 3T imaging
results.summary: 3T MRI with epilepsy protocol detects subtle hippocampal sclerosis missed on 1.5T in approximately 15-20% of cases initially reported as MRI-negative.

output.summary: Temporal lobe seizures presenting with prominent emotional and autonomic symptoms without convulsive activity are frequently misdiagnosed as panic attacks or anxiety, with diagnostic delays averaging 2-5 years. Prolonged video-EEG monitoring is essential when routine EEG is equivocal. High-field (3T) MRI with dedicated epilepsy protocol detects subtle hippocampal sclerosis missed on standard 1.5T in approximately 15-20% of cases initially reported as MRI-negative.

ground_truth.primary_diagnosis: Focal epilepsy of right temporal lobe origin with mesial temporal sclerosis (focal-onset seizures with impaired awareness)

differential.key_features: Pre-existing anxiety diagnosis raises possibility; however stereotyped semiology, post-ictal confusion, and cheek biting argue against pure PNES. Definitive distinction requires video-EEG capture of an event.
Patient carries an anxiety diagnosis and describes depersonalization, but the brief stereotyped behavioral arrest with oroalimentary automatisms and post-ictal confusion is not typical of panic.
Hypermotor or bizarre nocturnal events would suggest frontal-lobe origin; this patient's epigastric aura and oroalimentary automatisms localize to temporal lobe.
No prodromal lightheadedness, no postural trigger; post-event confusion is too prolonged for syncope.
Prior migraine without aura, but current events lack the gradual visual or sensory march and feature altered awareness with automatisms.

optimal_actions.action: Obtain detailed seizure history including semiology, aura, automatisms, duration, frequency, witness accounts, and post-ictal features.
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Stereotyped focal impaired-awareness events with temporal-lobe aura and post-ictal confusion.
Interictal exam typically normal; subtle memory deficit may be present.

optimal_actions.action: Obtain brain MRI using a dedicated epilepsy protocol to identify a structural epileptogenic cause
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Hippocampal sclerosis, low-grade tumor (DNET, ganglioglioma), cavernoma, or focal cortical dysplasia; rule out alternative structural causes.

optimal_actions.action: Search current literature for AED selection in focal epilepsy and ILAE 2017 seizure classification.
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Evidence-based AED options for focal epilepsy (levetiracetam, lamotrigine, oxcarbazepine, lacosamide); ILAE classification framework.

optimal_actions.action: Check drug interactions before initiating or modifying AED therapy (enzyme inducers, OCP, other CNS-active drugs).
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Identify pharmacokinetic interactions (CYP induction by carbamazepine/phenytoin) and CNS adverse-effect overlap.

optimal_actions.expected_finding: Interictal focal temporal discharges may support the clinical diagnosis

optimal_actions.expected_finding: Sleep may activate focal temporal epileptiform discharges

optimal_actions.expected_finding: Answer the specific provocation or treatment question in this presentation

useless_tools.rationale: No clinical features of CNS infection, encephalitis, or immunocompromise; CSF analysis is not indicated for routine focal epilepsy workup and exposes the patient to procedural risk and cost.
No syncope-versus-seizure question and no structural-heart concern; echocardiogram contributes nothing to epilepsy workup.
Ambulatory cardiac monitoring is reserved for syncope-versus-seizure differentiation; not indicated when semiology is clearly epileptic.
Non-contrast head CT is inferior to MRI for detecting epileptogenic substrates (hippocampal sclerosis, FCD, low-grade tumor) and adds ionizing radiation without diagnostic yield.

sequence_constraints.reason: Structural cause influences AED choice (e.g., low-grade tumor → consider AEDs with CYP-neutral profile; hippocampal sclerosis → multiple equally appropriate options). MRI should inform drug selection.

critical_actions: Recognize that stereotyped behavioral arrest with oroalimentary or manual automatisms and post-ictal confusion is a focal impaired-awareness seizure, not a panic attack.
Pursue prolonged video-EEG monitoring when routine EEG is equivocal and clinical suspicion remains high.
Repeat MRI with dedicated 3T epilepsy protocol (thin coronal cuts through the hippocampi) when standard MRI is equivocal.
Initiate an appropriate first-line AED for focal epilepsy (levetiracetam, lamotrigine, oxcarbazepine, or lacosamide) after diagnosis is confirmed.
Counsel the patient on driving restrictions, seizure-safety precautions, and sleep hygiene.
Reassess the prior anxiety diagnosis in light of the new epilepsy diagnosis.
contraindicated_actions: Do not dismiss the events as anxiety or panic without neurological workup.
Do not escalate sertraline or add benzodiazepines as anxiolytics in lieu of epilepsy evaluation.
Do not perform lumbar puncture — no clinical indication for CSF analysis.
Do not prescribe bupropion (lowers seizure threshold) for any indication.
Do not clear the patient to drive without observing the locally applicable seizure-free interval.
key_reasoning_points: Stereotypy and post-ictal confusion are the cardinal features distinguishing focal impaired-awareness seizures from psychogenic or anxiety-driven events.
Subtle epigastric aura and depersonalization are well-described temporal-lobe aura equivalents and are frequently mislabeled as anxiety.
An equivocal routine EEG does not exclude epilepsy; prolonged monitoring captures a habitual event in ~50–70% of definite cases.
Subtle hippocampal sclerosis can be missed on 1.5T; dedicated 3T epilepsy-protocol MRI catches additional lesions in 15–20% of MRI-negative cases.
Remote febrile seizure in childhood is a recognized risk factor for subsequent mesial temporal sclerosis and lends weight to the diagnosis.
Cross-modal concordance (right temporal EEG focus, right hippocampal sclerosis on 3T, right temporal hypometabolism on FDG-PET, visuospatial memory deficit) confirms localization.
Tier per the July 2026 clinical review: Laboratory testing does not diagnose focal epilepsy; it addresses a provoked seizure or a metabolic mimic when one is suspected.

July 2026 review applied end to end: routine EEG first when appropriate, staged sleep-deprived/ambulatory escalation, video only for event capture or tertiary evaluation, and continuous ICU EEG only for NCSE.

red_herrings.data_point: Two non-specific 2–3 mm T2/FLAIR-hyperintense foci in right frontal subcortical white matter on the initial 1.5T MRI.
red_herrings.intended_effect: Anchor on white-matter foci and pursue a demyelinating or vascular workup, missing the subtle hippocampal asymmetry.
red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Non-specific small white-matter foci are common, do not enhance, and are clinically silent here. Focus belongs on the hippocampal asymmetry that warrants 3T epilepsy-protocol MRI.

red_herrings.data_point: Pre-existing anxiety disorder with recent sertraline dose escalation and 'depersonalization' during episodes.
red_herrings.intended_effect: Attribute the episodes to anxiety / panic and increase psychotropic dose without neurological workup.
red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Stereotyped behavioral arrest with automatisms and post-ictal confusion is a focal-aware-then-impaired-awareness seizure, not panic; anxiety diagnosis must be revisited.

red_herrings.data_point: Mildly equivocal sharp transients on routine 45-min EEG, classified as 'not clearly epileptiform.'
red_herrings.intended_effect: Conclude EEG is normal and dismiss the epilepsy hypothesis.
red_herrings.correct_interpretation: A single equivocal routine EEG has 25–50% sensitivity. Prolonged video-EEG is needed when clinical suspicion is high.
